studies.Reference: Association between fish oil supplementation and cancer risk according to fatty fish consumption: A large prospective population-based cohort study using UK Biobank.
studies.Authors: Liu Z, Luo Y, Ren J, Yang L, Li J, Wei Z, He Y, Wang J, Li R, He L, Mu X, Huang Y, Song H, Hu X, Peng X
studies.comparison_type: Fish oil supplementation vs no supplementation, among participants consuming fatty fish at least two times per week

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: From the UK Biobank cohort, 470 804 participants with fish oil supplementation data were included.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: a higher risk of breast cancer was observed (HR = 1.16, 95% CI = 1.01-1.32)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: a higher risk of breast cancer was observed
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: a higher risk of breast cancer was observed

studies.Reference: Specialty supplements and breast cancer risk in the VITamins And Lifestyle (VITAL) Cohort.
studies.Authors: Brasky TM, Lampe JW, Potter JD, Patterson RE, White E
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants were queried on their recency (current versus past), frequency (days/week), and duration (years) of specialty supplement use.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Postmenopausal women, ages 50 to 76 years, who were residents of western Washington State, completed a 24-page baseline questionnaire in 2000 to 2002 (n = 35,016).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Current use of fish oil was associated with reduced risk of breast cancer (HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.50-0.92).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Current use of fish oil was associated with reduced risk of breast cancer
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Ten-year average use was suggestive of reduced risk (P trend = 0.09).
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Incident invasive breast cancers (n = 880) from 2000 to 2007 were obtained from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results registry.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Participants were queried on their recency (current versus past), frequency (days/week), and duration (years) of specialty supplement use.

studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: The erythrocyte phospholipid fatty acid composition was determined by gas-liquid chromatography, and the n-3 index was calculated with the percentage of eicosapentaenoic acid plus docosahexaenoic acid in total fatty acids.

headline.funnel_interpretation: The significant funnel plot asymmetry (egger's p=0.0200) indicates substantial publication bias in this meta-analysis on fish oil and breast cancer. This specific pattern suggests that smaller studies with smaller or null effects may be underrepresented, compromising the reliability of the pooled estimate and potentially leading to an overestimation of the true association.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 6 studies yielded an effect size of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.56–1.02), indicating no statistically significant association between fish oil and breast cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 82.42%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
